newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam prepares for Albright visit.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam prepares for Albright visit.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was due to arrive in Vietnam late on Thursday on a visit aimed at strengthening ties between the former foes.
But as teams of government officials and press officers made last minute preparations for her two-day trip, it was being overshadowed by events surrounding her agenda elsewhere in Asia.

At short notice, a two-day visit to Cambodia, scheduled to begin on Saturday, was cancelled because of what U.S. officials described as a "serious and unpredictable" security environment in Phnom Penh.

A State Department spokesman told reporters accompanying Albright that concerns over security following a firefight on June 17 between bodyguards loyal to co-prime ministers Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh had not subsided and the situation would not permit a visit.
The decision drew a statement of regret from Ranariddh who told reporters in Phnom Penh he had wanted to discuss "a number of major issues" with her.

U.S. officials said Albright would now stay in Vietnam until Saturday before travelling to Hong Kong a day earlier than previously planned to attend handover events surrounding the British colony's return to Chinese sovereignty on June 30.

Her visit is the second by a U.S. Secretary of State since the Vietnam War ended in 1975 with the fall of U.S.-backed Saigon and the climactic evacuation of U.S. personnel by helicopter from the rooftop of the American embassy in Saigon.
Warren Christopher visited two years to officiate at ceremonies surrounding the normalisation of diplomatic ties.

Albright is scheduled to meet with Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and Communist Party Chief Do Muoi on Friday. She is also expected to visit what remains of the Saigon embassy and lay a cornerstone marking the start of work on a new U.S. consulate.

U.S. officials say a priority issue for talks will be progress in efforts to account for the 2,100 missing American servicemen in Indochina. However she will also examine economic relations, sign a copyright accord, and discuss the thorny issue of human rights.

In an interview with Reuters earlier this week Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam said he would welcome dialogue on the issue as long as it was not used as a pretext for interference in Vietnam's internal affairs.
"An exchange of views helps to further understanding," he said. "But it (human rights) should not be used as a precondition for progress in other areas."
